newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish fin min sees interest rates staying low.
newsitem.headline: Finnish fin min sees interest rates staying low.

text.p: Finland's finance ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that interest rates should remain low and scant inflation pressures would keep interest rate expectations low also in the longer term.
The ministry's economics department said five-year government bond yields would fall to on average 5.1 percent this year from 6.0 percent in 1996.
At 1300/1100 GMT, the 10.75-percent government housing bond yielded 4.70 percent.
The ministry saw the three-month Helibor market rate, at 3.1 percent on average this year, down from 3.6 percent in 1996.
At the Bank of Finland's daily fixing at 1300/1100 GMT, the three-month Helibor rate was 3.07 percent.

The interest rate figures are "assumptions, not really forecasts," a senior finance ministry official said by telephone. The ministry's growth and other forecasts are built around the interest rate assumptions, he said.
"Our view is that the interest rate level in Europe might first fall slightly, and at the end of this year or early next year there could start to be upward pressures," he said.

In the new economic bulletin, the ministry said growth in Europe would accelerate "with substantially lower interest rates supporting a recovery in demand. Fiscal policy will remain tight, as efforts to balance public finances continue," it said.
"The surplus in the current account and the lower state budget deficit will keep interest rates low and Finnish financial markets buoyant," the ministry said.
"Inflationary pressures are minor, and this will keep interest rate expectations low also in the longer term," it added.
The 1997 C/A surplus would be 17.2 billion markka or 2.9 percent of GDP, down from 19.5 billion or 3.4 percent of GDP last year, according to the forecast.

"The condition of state finances will clearly improve this year, with strong economic growth increasing tax revenues and expenditure steering a moderate course in line with adopted savings programmes," it said.
